posts.quote: I can’t remember what I did yesterday. But play two seconds of an ’80s song and my brain pulls up the full file.
posts.caption: Yesterday is a blur. I could not tell you what I had for lunch or whether I ever called the pharmacy back. Then the grocery store played four notes of a song I last heard at a roller rink in 1986, and I knew every word. The harmony part too. I sang it in the cereal aisle while a teenager stocking shelves watched me like I was a weather event. My memory isn't failing. It's just very particular about what it keeps. The pharmacy is not in the file. Bon Jovi has his own folder.
posts.first: Last Saturday my husband asked where I put the checkbook. No idea. Ten minutes later the radio played a song from my junior prom and I told him the DJ's name, what I wore, and who cried in the parking lot. He found the checkbook himself. It was in the freezer.

posts.quote: My idea of a wild night now is going to bed and not looking at the clock until morning. Just out here living the dream.
posts.caption: Friday night I was in bed by 9:20. Not tired, just done. I put the phone across the room, turned the clock around so it faced the wall, and told my body it was on its own. And then something happened that hasn't happened since Cheers was still on the air. I slept straight through. No 2 a.m. ceiling stare, no 4 a.m. mental grocery list. I woke up to actual daylight and lay there like I'd won a contest. I told three people about it before lunch. Two of them were jealous. The third one asked what my secret was.
posts.first: My secret was nothing. I didn't do anything different. I'm just going to keep turning the clock around and hoping it works again. So far it has worked once in eleven tries. I'm still counting that as a strategy.

posts.quote: I don’t hold grudges. I just remember everything, forever, in perfect detail.
posts.caption: My cousin brought up the potato salad incident at Thanksgiving like it was ancient history. It was 2011. She said I took it personally. I did not take it personally. I took it accurately. I remember the bowl, the lid that didn't fit, and the exact tone she used when she said she 'improved' my recipe. I've forgiven her, in the sense that I still come to Thanksgiving. I have not forgotten, in the sense that I bring my own potato salad and set it a respectful distance from hers. That's not a grudge. That's a seating chart.
posts.first: My husband says I have a memory like a filing cabinet. He means it as a compliment, mostly. He also knows I can tell him exactly what he said about my mother on Labor Day weekend in 1999, word for word, including the hand gesture. He doesn't bring up 1999 anymore.

posts.quote: My knees now make a noise every time I stand up. It’s not pain. It’s commentary.
posts.caption: I sat on the floor to look for a lid in the bottom cabinet. That was my first mistake. Getting down was fine. Getting back up sounded like somebody stepping on bubble wrap in a quiet library. My husband asked from the other room if I'd dropped something. I said no, that was me. At this point my knees narrate everything. Standing up from the couch, a little click. Getting out of the car, a full sentence. Climbing the stairs with laundry, an opinion. I'm not in pain. They just have a lot to say lately.
posts.first: At my last checkup the doctor asked me to squat and stand. My left knee made a noise so loud the nurse looked up from her computer. The doctor said it was perfectly normal. Then she wrote something down. I'd still like to know what she wrote.

posts.quote: I’m at the stage where my hair needs more maintenance than my car, and honestly my car has been more cooperative.

posts.first: This year's was green leather with gold corners and a ribbon. I wrote in it for nine days. It's now holding my place in a magazine at a page about lemon chicken. I have never made lemon chicken. I'm already looking at next year's planners.

posts.quote: Every invitation gets the same three questions. How long is it? Will there be parking? Can I leave early without anyone noticing?
posts.caption: An invitation came in the mail on Tuesday. Real paper, a little gold border, the works. My first feeling wasn't excitement. It was logistics. I flipped it over looking for an end time and there wasn't one, which is how they get you. I looked up the address and it's one of those neighborhoods where everybody parks on the lawn. I texted my friend Donna to see if she was going, mostly so I'd have someone to leave with. She texted back the same three questions I had. We've been friends for thirty years for a reason.
posts.first: Donna and I have a system now. We arrive together, stay exactly ninety minutes, and one of us says 'oh, the dog' at the door. Neither of us has a dog. Nobody has ever asked a follow-up question about the dog.

posts.quote: We grew up drinking from the garden hose and riding in the back of pickup trucks. Now I need a 45-minute YouTube video to put together a lawn chair.
posts.caption: When I was nine I rode in the bed of my uncle's truck forty miles to the lake, holding a cooler and a dog, and nobody thought twice about it. We drank warm water out of the hose that tasted like pennies and sunshine. We were tough. Last Sunday I bought a lawn chair. One lawn chair. It came in a box with eleven parts, a bag of screws, and instructions drawn by someone who hates me. I watched a man named Gary explain it for forty-five minutes. I paused Gary six times. The chair works now. Mostly. It leans a little to the left.
posts.first: There was one screw left over when I finished. I put it in the kitchen drawer with the other mystery screws from every piece of furniture I've ever owned. I sat in the chair anyway. It held. I'm choosing not to think about where that screw was supposed to go.

posts.quote: Cancelled plans are like finding twenty dollars in an old coat, except the twenty dollars is my whole evening.
posts.caption: At 4:52 on Wednesday my friend texted that she had to cancel dinner. Her kid had something, she was so sorry, could we rain-check. I typed back 'no worries at all!' with an exclamation point, which is the only exclamation point I've used since August. Then I sat on the edge of the bed and felt it. That rush. The whole evening, just handed back to me. I had already put on real pants. I took them off ceremonially. Leftover soup, a blanket, and two episodes of a show about people renovating houses I could never afford.
posts.first: She texted again around eight to apologize one more time. I told her truly, it was fine. I didn't tell her I was already in my robe with the heating pad. Some things you keep to yourself. We rescheduled for next week. I'm hoping something comes up.

posts.quote: I opened the fridge, stood there for a full minute, and closed it. I wasn’t hungry. I just needed to check on everybody.
posts.caption: It was 9:40 on a Tuesday and I wasn't even a little hungry. I'd eaten dinner. I'd had a cookie I wasn't going to mention. Still, I walked into the kitchen and opened the fridge like a night nurse doing rounds. The leftover lasagna was holding up. The half lemon was not. The pickles were fine, the pickles are always fine. I stood there in the cold glow with the door wide open, letting all the cold out, exactly the way my father told me never to do. Then I closed it, satisfied. Everybody was accounted for.
posts.first: My husband caught me doing it once and asked what I was looking for. I said nothing. He said then why is the door open. I didn't have an answer for him. I still don't. The lemon went in the trash the next morning. It had a good run.

posts.quote: My weekend plans include a blanket, a show I’ve already seen twice, and absolutely no one asking me what’s for dinner.

I have fed people for thirty-one years. This weekend the kitchen is closed.
posts.first: Last Sunday I made it until 5:38 before anyone asked. That's a personal record. I pointed at the pantry without looking away from the TV. He made himself a sandwich. It was a perfectly good sandwich. Nobody starved. Everybody survived the weekend, including me.

posts.quote: I wrote myself a reminder so I wouldn’t forget. Now I can’t remember where I put the reminder.
posts.caption: Sunday night I knew I'd forget to call about the furnace, so I did the responsible thing. I wrote it down. Big letters, yellow sticky note, 'CALL FURNACE GUY.' I remember being proud of myself. Monday came and went. Tuesday afternoon I suddenly remembered that I had written a reminder, which is not the same as remembering what it said or where it went. I checked the fridge, the coffee maker, my purse, the car visor. Nothing. On Wednesday it was cold in the house. That's how I remembered the furnace.
posts.first: Found the sticky note Thursday. It was stuck to the bottom of my reading glasses case, which was in the bathroom, for reasons I won't be investigating. The furnace guy is coming Monday. I wrote that down too. On my hand this time. In pen.
